choices.A: A new label for the drawer
choices.B: A small wrapped box
choices.C: A borrowed desk lamp
choices.D: A piece of the discarded sign

questions.explanation: The brother returns carrying a small wrapped box and asks the narrator to keep his present in the same hiding place.
questions.stimulusText:
I hid Dad's birthday present in the bottom drawer of my desk. The problem was that my brother sometimes borrowed things from that desk. To discourage him, I made a label in my most ordinary handwriting: NOTHING INTERESTING.
Then I waited for the drawer to become invisible.
That afternoon, I heard my brother reading the label aloud.
"Why does this one need to tell me?" he asked.
"It contains ordinary things."
He pointed to the two unmarked drawers above it. "What do those contain?"
"Ordinary things too."
He looked pleased, as though I had just supplied the missing piece of a puzzle. I suddenly understood that the label had advertised exactly what I wanted hidden.
After he left, I took it off. The desk looked like a desk again. I was putting the paper in the wastebasket when he returned carrying a small wrapped box.
"Since you've chosen a secret place," he said, "could you keep my present in there too?"
I opened the drawer just wide enough to admit his parcel without revealing mine.
"Don't tell Dad."
"I didn't need you to tell me that."
By dinner, the drawer was private again, although it now had two managers. My brother and I agreed that our improved system required no sign at all.

questions.prompt: What helps hold selected portions of the worm against the soil?

choices.A: Tiny bristles
choices.B: Rigid walking legs
choices.C: A hard outer shell
choices.D: Wings along each segment

questions.correctAnswer: Tiny bristles
questions.explanation: The passage identifies tiny bristles as structures that help selected parts grip the surrounding soil during coordinated movement.
questions.stimulusText:
An earthworm moves forward without legs by coordinating changes in its body's shape with a grip on the ground. Its body consists of fluid-filled segments surrounded by muscles. Because the fluid does not readily compress, changing one dimension of a segment affects another.
Circular muscles form bands around a segment. When one of these bands contracts, it narrows the segment and makes it longer. Muscles running along the body work differently: their contraction makes segments shorter and thicker. Alternating these actions lets different portions extend and shorten.
Shape changes alone, however, do not guarantee forward travel. Tiny bristles help hold selected parts against the surrounding soil. With a rear portion anchored, a front portion can lengthen forward. The front can then grip while shortening behind it draws more of the body ahead. Coordinated waves of activity pass along the worm rather than moving every segment in exactly the same way at once.
The bristles are not miniature walking legs. They provide contact that allows muscular changes to produce useful movement against the ground. On a very slippery surface, muscles might still change the body's shape while less of that motion carries the entire animal forward. The explanation therefore requires both internal changes and an external grip: one creates reach and pulling movement, while the other prevents those movements from simply sliding back.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Missing Line on the Plan
questions.stimulusText:
A plan of a public square shows paths meeting at neat right angles. After several months, a narrow track appears diagonally across the grass. No designer drew that line. Repeated footsteps made it visible. Such an informal path records a choice people have made, not merely a route someone intended them to follow.
The worn track can teach a designer something important. Perhaps the paved route takes people far out of their way between a bus stop and an entrance. The diagonal reveals that some users value a shorter connection. Ignoring it would mean overlooking evidence about how the square is actually used.
Should every worn track therefore become a paved path? The question is more difficult than the bare line suggests. A muddy shortcut may serve some walkers while excluding people who need a firm, level surface. Its visible users do not represent everyone who might cross the square. A route may also interfere with another important use of the space.
The track is consequently evidence to investigate, rather than a complete design instruction. A thoughtful response might preserve its useful connection while changing its surface or position. Plans express intentions; worn paths reveal some results. Good design can learn from the difference without pretending that either the plan or the track tells the entire story.

choices.B: The purchase of a kitchen table

questions.stimulusText:
Grandfather set a postcard on the kitchen table and asked me to write to Emil, whom he had not seen since the ferry service closed. "Just a few words," he said. He began with the weather.
Before I finished the first line, the weather had become the winter when the ferry rope froze. That led to a passenger who carried a live rooster, and the rooster led to Emil's peculiar way of laughing without opening his mouth. Grandfather demonstrated. My pen stopped.
"Should I put that in?" I asked.
"Naturally. He'll remember."
I drew a line through my opening and wrote smaller. Soon my letters leaned against one another like passengers in the old ferry. Grandfather was now describing the day Emil repaired the landing with boards taken from his own shed. This, apparently, required an explanation of the shed.
"We need a smaller story," I said.
Grandfather considered the postcard. "Or more paper."
I found an envelope and several blank sheets. When he began again, I stopped crossing things out. The shed acquired a roof, a smell of apples, and a door that never quite shut.
The postcard remained beside us. It still said only "Dear Emil." For the first time that afternoon, its emptiness did not seem like a problem.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what produces the decrease in brightness during a planetary transit?

questions.stimulusText:
A distant planet may be too faint to appear separately beside its bright star. Astronomers can sometimes detect it indirectly, however, by recording how much light reaches a telescope from the star over time. If the planet passes between the telescope and the star, it hides a small portion of the star's visible surface. The recorded brightness briefly decreases.
This crossing is called a transit. A planet that returns along the same orbit can produce regularly spaced dips. The spacing supplies evidence about how long one orbit takes. The depth of a dip, under suitable observing conditions, helps estimate the planet's size relative to the star: a larger blocking disk generally hides more of the star's light.
A dip alone does not establish that a planet is present. Another star crossing in front of the observed star can also reduce the received light. Dark regions on a rotating star can produce changing brightness as well. Astronomers therefore examine the pattern and seek other observations that can distinguish these explanations.
The method also has a built-in limitation. An orbit tilted away from the observer's line of sight may never carry its planet across the visible star. Such a planet can exist without producing any transit for that observer. A steady brightness record is therefore not a complete inventory of the star's planets.

questions.stimulusTitle: Opening a Path Through the Threads
questions.stimulusText:
On a simple loom, one set of threads is held lengthwise under tension. These threads are called the warp. A second thread, the weft, travels across them. Weaving requires more than laying the weft on top: the two sets must repeatedly cross over and under one another so that the growing cloth holds together.
For plain weave, the loom separates alternate warp threads into two groups. Lifting one group opens a space between the groups, called a shed. A shuttle carries the weft through that opening. The loom then reverses which group is raised, and the shuttle makes another pass. A warp thread that lay above one weft pass consequently lies below the next. This alternation produces the basic interlacing pattern.
After a pass, the newest weft is pressed toward the cloth already formed. Without this step, successive passes would remain too far apart for the intended fabric. Warp tension helps keep the lengthwise threads in useful positions while the shed opens and closes.
The shuttle transports the crossing thread, but it does not choose the pattern by itself. The order in which groups of warp threads rise and fall determines which crossings occur. More elaborate grouping and lifting arrangements can produce other patterns. In this way, a repeated sequence of openings becomes an arrangement that remains visible after the openings themselves have disappeared.

Della found the green glove on the bench outside the skating rink. She had lost one like it that morning, and for a moment the sight seemed to settle everything. She put her cold hand inside.
Two letters scratched her wrist. She turned back the cuff and found J.M. stitched into the wool. She did not remember any initials in her own gloves.

She pulled the glove off.
"Is this it?"
He checked the cuff. "Yes. Thanks."
There was no speech about honesty. He hurried toward the person waiting by the gate, and Della was left with one cold hand again.
She returned to the bench and looked underneath it. Her own glove was still missing, but now she knew which one she was searching for.

questions.stimulusTitle: Two Sides of a Mountain Range
questions.stimulusText:
Two valleys can lie at similar heights on opposite sides of a mountain range yet receive very different amounts of rain. One reason is the route taken by moisture-bearing air. The prevailing wind, meaning the wind that most often comes from a particular direction, carries that air toward one side of the range.
As the air rises along the mountains, it expands and cools. Cooling can cause some of its water vapor to condense into droplets. Clouds may form, and some water can fall as rain or snow before the air crosses the highest ground. The side facing the incoming wind therefore often receives more precipitation.
Beyond the crest, the air descends. Descending air becomes warmer, making condensation less likely. It may also have already lost part of its water on the first side. The valley beyond the range can consequently be much drier, a situation called a rain shadow. A mountain does not need to act like a solid wall that stops every cloud for this contrast to develop.
This explanation describes a recurring pattern, not a promise about every storm. Winds can shift, and other sources of moisture can affect either valley. Nor does every dry region lie in a rain shadow. To decide whether the pattern helps explain a particular place, one must consider both the surrounding landforms and the usual journey of its incoming air.

questions.stimulusText:
Imagine marking a grain of sand near the foot of a moving dune and watching it through many windy afternoons. The dune does not roll forward as one solid block. Its outline changes through the accumulated movement of separate grains.
Wind strong enough to move loose sand can push grains along the ground or lift them into short hops. Some travel up the dune's exposed slope. Near the crest, its highest ridge, they may pass over to the more sheltered side. Sand collecting there can become steep enough to slip downward in small avalanches.
Repeated transfers remove material from the windward side and deposit it beyond the ridge. With a persistent wind direction, the dune's crest and sheltered slope can gradually shift forward. A photograph taken much later may show the familiar shape standing in a new position, although individual grains have followed separate routes and may have stopped at different places.
Our marked grain might become buried partway through this process. Another grain could pass over the ridge sooner. Tracking one grain therefore describes that grain's journey; comparing the dune's outline at different times describes a changing landform. These are related observations, but they answer different questions.
Vegetation or insufficient wind can hold much sand in place. The movement described here depends on grains being loose enough to travel and on wind repeatedly transporting them.

Tracking one grain therefore describes that grain's journey; comparing the dune's outline at different times describes a changing landform. These are related observations, but they answer different questions.

questions.stimulusText:
Consider a repairer working with fittings made individually in different workshops. A nut that fits one screw may resist another that looks almost identical. Diameter alone does not settle the matter: the spacing and shape of the threads must match as well. The repairer may spend time altering the replacement until the particular pair works.
An agreed set of dimensions changes the work. A maker can produce a fitting to a stated specification, and a distant repairer can select a replacement using that same specification. Each pair no longer needs its own private history of adjustment. The benefit extends beyond the object itself: people who have never met can coordinate through shared measurements.
Such agreements also demand work. Makers must check their tools, inspect the resulting pieces, and decide how much variation is acceptable. This permitted variation is a tolerance. A dimension written on paper accomplishes little unless production remains within its stated limits. Changing an established system can also leave old stock incompatible with new pieces.
Standardization thus redirects skilled judgment toward selecting dimensions, setting limits, and maintaining repeatable production. A rule can make parts interchangeable within its system while leaving other systems different. Shared dimensions function like a common language for a particular exchange; their usefulness depends on the participants agreeing on what its signs mean.
